title: Small Language Models Run Out of Context Before They Run Out of Smarts
dek: A field guide to shipping a model that fits in a pocket: spend the prompt carefully, scaffold the reasoning, prove the port and lock the weights for real.
by: Draft for team review · written by Claude Code from published research and engineering writing · checked in code
lead: What is a small language model? One compact enough to run on your own device. It earns its place when you budget its context, scaffold its reasoning, verify the port and protect the weights.

cover.alt: Two phones: one overflowing with text token tiles, one holding a few compact embedding rows with room to spare.
cover.caption: The same sensor window costs a small model very different amounts of context as text and as embeddings.

description: What is a small language model, and how do you ship one on a device? Context budgets, scaffolding, parity checks and weight protection.
keywords: what is a small language model
decisions: Encode non-text signals as embeddings, never as printed digits
Scaffold a small model before upsizing it
Gate every port on token-level parity with a reference
Treat output-only weight obfuscation as unprotected
Keep hybrid device-cloud designs out of privacy-critical paths

body.text: Stop pasting raw sensor samples into the prompt

body: Here's the most common way an on-device model goes wrong. You have a phone, a stream of sensor readings and a small model that fits in memory. So you print the samples as text and paste them into the prompt. It works on a short clip. Then a longer window arrives. A new arXiv paper on PocketTSLM names the result: text inputs «exhaust the context and memory budgets of small on-device models».

Why does text hurt so much? Every sample becomes several tokens: digits, a decimal point, a separator. The context window, the span of tokens a model can attend to at once, fills with punctuation. Prefill, the pass that reads the whole prompt before the first output token, grows with it. Summarising the stream into averages is the other escape. It saves room. It also flattens the timing you needed.

We went through the PocketTSLM design step by step. An encoder turns each time-series window into a short run of vectors. Those enter the model as embeddings, the internal vectors a token would normally become. That's a soft prompt: input the model reads without it ever being text. The phone app works «by injecting encoded time-series windows as embeddings instead of tokenizing time series as text».

Follow one clip through. A 30-second Sleep-EDF EEG clip needs a sleep stage. As embeddings, it uses «approximately 12 times fewer time-series tokens» and less prefill. As text, longer windows «exceed the phone's context or memory budget». Nothing leaves the phone either: «no health data transmitted during inference». We think this is the default for any non-text signal. Encode it; don't spell it out.

body.caption: The soft-prompt path keeps a sensor window off the text tokenizer entirely.
steps: A sensor window arrives on the phone
An encoder turns the window into vectors
The vectors enter the model as embeddings
The model prefills a short prompt
The answer decodes on the device

body.text: Scaffold the small model before you reach for a bigger one

body: Second trap. Your small model gives shaky answers, so you swap in a bigger one and lose the reason you went local. A new arXiv paper on CARE-SD takes another path. It starts from an honest premise: small models' «limited reasoning capabilities make simple prompting insufficient for context-aware and factually reliable analysis». The task is sensitive, too: spotting self-disclosures in cybersecurity interviews that must stay on local machines.

body.alt: A small model at the centre of four checking modules that pass an interview clockwise from input to labelled output.
body.caption: CARE-SD wraps a small model in four stages, and the checking lives in the stages, not in the model.

body: the 3B model matched the 20B reference model in category Macro-F1

The fix is plumbing. CARE-SD is a «four-module architecture integrating context-adaptive processing, hierarchical disclosure reasoning, explanation-consistency verification, and cross-batch reconciliation». Read it as a pipeline. One stage fits the prompt to the interview's context. One reasons from broad category to narrow. One checks that each explanation supports its label. The last reconciles verdicts across batches, so a long interview split into chunks stays consistent.

Now the surprise. With the scaffold, Llama 3B's Macro-F1 went from 0.80 to 0.88, and unsupported claims fell by 60%. Macro-F1 averages the F1 score per category, so rare categories count as much as common ones. Then the kicker: «the 3B model matched the 20B reference model in category Macro-F1». We agree with the direction. Our caveat is scope: one task, 82 annotated interviews, careful human review behind every number.

body.text: Prove the port matches the reference, token for token

body: Porting is where small models break without telling you. You convert the weights, swap the runtime, maybe lower the numeric precision. The output still reads fluently. Fluent isn't identical. A small drift in the logits, the raw scores a model gives each candidate next token, can flip one choice. Every token after it then follows a different path.

PocketTSLM treats this as a gate. «A numerical parity protocol verifies identical greedy-decoded token sequences between the Swift port and a Python reference». Greedy decoding always takes the top-scoring token, so sampling noise drops out of the comparison. Same input, same tokens, or the port is broken. It's cheap to run on every build, and it's strict.

A second line in that paper deserves copying. Against another reference, the bar was looser: «Answers also match the PyTorch reference, although rationale wording can differ». We think that split is exactly right. Pin token-level parity where the runtime allows it. Where it can't, compare answers and tolerate drift in the explanation. Then write down which bar each build passed.

body.text: Count what leaves the phone when the server joins in

body: Some jobs outgrow the device. Device-cloud speculative decoding is the usual compromise. A small draft model on the phone guesses a few tokens ahead, and the large server model checks them in one parallel pass. The phone's chip is the bottleneck: a deep draft tree «requires repeated passes on a mobile neural processing unit (NPU)», says a new arXiv paper on HyCo.

body.alt: Phone and server zones split by a dashed boundary, with drafts crossing to the server and state returning.
body.caption: A device-cloud split shrinks the drafter to fit the chip and sends context across the device boundary.

body: We retraced what HyCo surrenders to fit. «Quantization, a restricted vocabulary, and a 1K-token window fit both drafters to the NPU.» Quantization stores weights at lower precision. A restricted vocabulary lets the drafter propose only a subset of tokens. The short window means it sees only recent text. Each is capability traded for memory, and each belongs in your eval notes.

The server bill falls. HyCo cut server GPU time per output token by «29.2% on 32K-token summarization», against the server drafting for itself. Now look at the privacy shape. PocketTSLM kept everything local. A split design needs the server to see the text it verifies. If you went on-device for privacy, a hybrid quietly gives that back.

body.text: Assume anyone holding the phone can study your weights

body: Shipping a model to a phone means shipping its weights. Anyone holding the phone can try to read them. A Trusted Execution Environment, or TEE, is a hardware-isolated enclave whose code the rest of the device can't inspect. Enclaves are cramped, so designs shield only part of the model and disguise the rest. That disguise is weight obfuscation: exposed matrices multiplied by a secret transform.

body.alt: Left, a weight matrix disguised on one side with a single key that fits; right, both sides disguised and many keys fit.
body.caption: One-sided obfuscation leaves exactly one key that fits; two-sided obfuscation hides it among many.

body: hiding the true key among many equally valid candidates

The BiShield-TEE authors say most such schemes rely on «unilateral matrix transformations that obfuscate only output side». Their diagnosis is blunt: «the obfuscation secret is uniquely determined, exposing the structure of the true key and enabling attackers to break the protection». Picture a lock where exactly one key shape fits. Unique fit is a clue. Search long enough and the key gives itself away.

The damage isn't subtle. Representative methods «are reduced to negligible protection», with attacks «recovering near-complete model functionality». The fix is bilateral: obfuscate input and output dimensions jointly, «hiding the true key among many equally valid candidates». In our view, this resets the default threat model. Treat one-sided obfuscation as no protection at all until it survives this attack.

body.caption: One-sided and two-sided weight obfuscation inside a TEE partition.
rows: Held to the full-shielding black-box baseline

body.text: Leave the work in the cloud when nothing private or urgent is at stake

body: So when should you skip all this? When privacy and latency aren't your constraint. The BiShield-TEE paper opens by tying on-device adoption to «latency and privacy requirements». Take both away and a phone is a cramped, battery-bound server you don't control. You'd be paying every cost in this guide for nothing.

The cloud path has a fair case, and PocketTSLM states it: «Cloud-hosted time-series language models avoid smartphone limits». Their objection is that those models «repeatedly move sensitive physiology off the device and add latency and per-query compute cost». Strip out the sensitivity and the tight latency budget. Most of that objection goes with them.

Skip it, too, when you can't afford the checking. CARE-SD's gains came with annotated interviews and independent human review. Without that kind of scrutiny, a small model's mistakes stay invisible. And skip it when the weights are your crown jewels and one-sided obfuscation is your only shield. A small model you can't verify or protect is a liability that fits in a pocket.
What is a small language model?

A small language model is a compact model built to run on modest hardware, such as a phone or a local machine. CARE-SD evaluated local models from Llama 1B to Llama 3B. The appeal is control: sensitive data stays put and nothing waits on a network. The cost is weaker reasoning, so small models need structure around them and inputs designed for their limits.
Can small language models run fully on a phone?

Yes, when the input is designed for the device's memory. PocketTSLM «runs fully on a consumer smartphone by injecting encoded time-series windows as embeddings». Text-serialized baselines ran out of room at longer windows. Hybrid designs that verify drafts on a server also exist, but they send context off the phone, which changes the privacy story.
Are on-device LLM weights safe from extraction?

Not by default, and one-sided obfuscation inside a TEE looks breakable. The BiShield-TEE authors show the secret in those schemes «is uniquely determined, exposing the structure of the true key». Their bilateral design hides the key among many valid candidates and holds attack accuracy to the full-shielding black-box baseline. Treat weight protection as its own engineering task, with its own threat model.
